items.title: Wardogs presents a different kind of FPS power fantasy: making fat stacks as a pacifist rideshare driver
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer
items.text:
Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer shooter in which I’ve just found employment. Its "Play like to you used to" tagline and Halo 3-aping trailer smell a bit of reactionary, stuck-in-the-past thinking. It’s a mass-scale multiplayer shooter, so individual heroics rarely influence match outcomes. And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. Almost every positive action earns you cash, from the obvious hardpoint captures and squadmate revives to the humble delivery of people and bandages to the frontlines. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

In an accurate reflection of reality, you begin with little, must buy all vehicles and equipment yourself, and are on the hook if they’re lost while on duty. But the creation of genuine rear-detachment roles means Wardogs solves problems I have with both big shooters, and the extraction subgenre it also borrows from: by constantly ferrying teammates, I can have an individual yet materially important impact on the match, and by never intentionally joining a gunfight, I need never worry about loot loss anxiety. It was the perfect career move.

Buoyed by first-day enthusiasm, once I finally loaded into a game I bought a car, directed it dutifully towards the crowd of pedestrian soldiers, and immediately caused a helicopter crash. My pull-up-to-the-kerb manoeuvre had unwittingly put me in the landing path of a descending attack chopper – a major fault in the standard United Kingdom driving test – forcing the delicate warbird to flip over my roof and explode. Its occupants, miraculously unhurt but quite cross, shot me a damning glance as they strode off to buy another one.

The rest of my inaugural fare, a full house of one real-life friend and two silent randomers, went mercifully smoother. Despite the slippery handling of my entry-level SUV, it was a comfortable, peaceful drive towards the hot zone, which itself offered ample parking space for my passengers to hop out. The prizes came instantly: $1,000 for a "tactical deployment", plus $500 for each of my unharmed passengers, plus a $15 tip from a particularly satisfied rider. $2,515 for a few kilometres of relaxed cruising? The hell am I doing as a deputy ed?

The private hire lifestyle took hold. For multiple runs, I’d steer back to base, wait next to other transit vehicles (sometimes sharing an “A’ight, mate” with the heli pilot next to me), load up on balaclava men, and deliver them vaguely near the sound of gunfire, my balance swelling with each trip. Half an hour in, I’d accumulated slightly higher earnings than my IRL friend, who’d been running around murdering people and getting shot himself. Sounds painful. Sounds like participating directly in the horrors of war, mankind’s most terrible creation, and a blight on the Earth that continues to destroy families and erase cultures every day. Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

Meanwhile, my hands were clean, not counting all the filthy lucre that was crossing it. Granted, my usefulness was starting and ending with the thunk of automobile doors – sometimes I’d watch my disembarked comrades perish just moments after paying their fare, a tragically premature "Passenger survived, +$500" lingering onscreen as their heaped form shrunk in my rearview. In these moments I was less Iqbal, the friendly Prius owner who got me home from the pub last week, and more Charon, damned soul ferryman of the River Styx.

As the match went on, I also began having trouble with that key component of hypercapitalism: competition. It turned out those heli pilots were not my mates at all, but were conspiring to steal my business, adopting the unfair and likely illegal practice of having faster vehicles than me. Eventually, my stream of human tip jars reduced to a trickle of stragglers, the larger crowds routinely making a beeline for the nimbler, more spectacular choppers.

In search of alternative revenue streams, I diversified into supply logistics. At this point I hadn’t made quite enough profit to afford a proper truck, so instead bought one empty crate, chucked a few cheap medical supplies into it, and bunged it my car's back seat. Seemingly in ignorance of the massive boot, but whatever. I knew delivering it somewhere useful would require driving deeper into the fray than my people-carrying had thus far, but shareholder value (mine) demanded it.

The journey was, again, uneventful, and I chanced upon a makeshift base swarming with more action-inclined teammates. Surely, the kind of folk who’d appreciate a box of plasters. Not entirely familiar with the controls, I hit the G key to unload, at which point the create seemed to disappear. A "Supplies delivered, +$500" popped up – which, as my accountant tells me, if half what I could have made by filling those seats with bums instead – but I remained concerned about the supplies themselves. Beginning my search, I reversed, directly onto and over the bandage box that has been laying just out of view. Now, I was stuck, the car’s back end suspended barely high enough for the rear-wheel-drive wheels to regain purchase on the tarmac.

This was not ideal. As I got back at the wheel and tried wriggling free with Game Physics sorcery, I noticed the allies I’d come to resupply were no longer dashing around on the roof. Within seconds, a lone, green-dressed man with no 'Don’t shoot this one' arrow above his head rounded the building’s corner, rifle raised. Still stuck, I killed the engine and did the best impression of an empty, slightly slanted car that I’ll ever have to do. The man’s scope swivelled in my direction, then kept going, the ruse successful long enough for an arrowed teammate to pop out from behind a van and shoot him down.

Hands sweating in gratitude, I eventually managed to slide my bumper free and roar off back to HQ, alive and enriched. My shift was only brought to an end by a return of those blasted server errors, but I clocked off a happy man: I’d nearly tripled my net worth and had been, more so than in any Battlefield game I’ve ever bumbled through, helpful. Honestly, what a silly slogan – why play like you used to when you can start an exciting new career in personal transportation?

items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell

items.text:
The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute attrition, but the true Napoleon of Drag-Select knows that strategy is always, primarily, the mastery of time. I don't think Napoleon would have approved of Ex Sanguis. He would not have liked all the willowy clone women made out of congealed blood and pincers. He would have suspected them of being divorcees and Babouvists. But perhaps he would have appreciated the game's fixation with seizing the initiative.

As with Lightbulb's previous grid-based tactics RPG Othercide, Ex Sanguis has you going up against dozens of vaguely eschatological bladespawn with just the three austere and menacing bladegirls. There are generally a half-dozen foes to start with, and reinforcements soon hatch from gross eggsacs around the map. You can't simply overwhelm your opponents, then. Instead, you must pre-empt and interrupt them, anticipating their advance and dancing your best moves in first on the game's fluctuating timeline.

Some abilities are performed instantly, while others trigger after a delay. However initially inconvenient, the delays soon become an asset, as you learn to aim your artillery strikes where you know your enemies will be, a few score ticks from now. Other abilities trigger when an opponent acts, cutting them off. Or when a friendly deals some damage, adding a follow-up attack. A key question is whether to exhaust your regular action points and dip into your Burst bar, which lets you sneak in some extra licks at the cost of wildly postponing the character's next turn.

Watch on YouTube

And then there's repositioning: you get shoves, gravity pulses, and driving kicks that punt opponents around. This allows you to knock delayed enemy attacks off target, perhaps slamming the noxious seraphim into a boulder, or nudging them into the path of the AOE move you've just queued up with the previous character. As you preview these gambits, the character portraits and action indicators shuffle to and fro on the timeline. On higher difficulties, it's vitally important to avoid a scenario where the whole opposing force can take a turn, one after the other.

When I played Othercide, I didn't quite clock how much Lightbulb's approach has in common with Into The Breach. The resemblance feels a bit more prominent in Ex Sanguis. There's no fixed match countdown, true, but you're encouraged to finish fast: the angelbeasts are only going to get more numerous, and you generally aren't required to slaughter all of them - just a surgeon's handful of VIPs or a single enemy map fixture, sulking to the rear.

It's a messier experience than you'll find in Subset's game, however. The environments are full of blood blisters that blow up when struck, launching nearby characters a few squares. On more crowded maps, a single volatile pustule often triggers a prolonged cascade. The AI in the early access build seems overfond of setting the blisters off, in addition to controlling terrain. Some times, it's hellbent on swarming you; at others, it tries to lock down big portions of the map by preparing a delayed AOE move, wherever it finds itself.

The greater emphasis on terrain damage is one thing that distinguishes the early access version of Ex Sanguis from what I remember of Othercide. The other, more obvious point of departure is that Ex Sanguis has a trimmer roguelike structure, with more focussed progression.

On which note, here's my best effort at explaining the story: some kind of pesky vampire moon has leeched away the world's vital fluids and memories, reducing all of Creation to an ivory placeholder. You are the Mater, a goddess replete with the simmering intensity of Derek Zoolander. She can spawn duplicates of herself to fight the moon's minions. So far, it's very much the previous game's gothic mommy monster mash on fast-forward – all pout and glare and cod Latin metaphors, without much coherence but with a lot of enjoyable attitude.

It feels faster partly because there's less going on outside battle. Each run kicks you off with three warriors, allowing you to pick their classes – the initial options are broadly Swordlady, Gunlass and Time Wizardress - and starting abilities. You then trek across a cratered world map, fighting battles (with unlockable higher difficulties) and accumulating Corrupted Blood for campaign progression. Every battle you win nets you a choice of three further abilities or stat boosts per character.

Yes, we are operating in the realm of Vampire Survivors, just a teeny bit. As in the previous game and many other roguelikes, abilities form complementary sets, which are fun to unearth: for example, Swordlady can inflict bleed with one kind of melee attack, then slurp up the debuff to restore her own health. Eventually, you swill down enough Corrupted Blood from victories to access a bossfight, which functions as a chapter break. items.title: Skyrim’s official IKEA crossover mod might be the most deftly-assembled Elder Scrolls gag ever, if not an ad blueprint other corps should follow
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim
items.text:
I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim as an official Bethesda-approved Creation, that I’d now be sitting here noting that I dug said creation’s dungeon designs.

I am, though, because I think that sums up the entire experience of playing through Kallax Storageborn. If all you do is read a headline about it or scan through the premise with a smirk, you might assume it’s just a soulless corporate stunt aiming to play off The Elder Scrolls 5’s well-established viral memeality, but without any depth that makes it worth dedicating the time to check out. That was largely how I felt about it too, up until I learned that highly skilled Fallout 4 Sim Settlements makers Kinggath Creations were the modders behind the free creation, and decided to check their work out for myself.

The secondary motivation I had for doing so was that in-game advertising feels like it’s being floated more often than ever at the moment as a way games might help pay for themselves, as the squeeze is felt across an industry desperate for maximum financial returns. Fantasy RPGs like Skyrim are arguably among the toughest places to naturally fit such ads, especially compared to the likes of sports games or James Bond adventures with special watches.

In terms of how it fits in Tamriel, you’ll probably be glad to learn that outside of loosely meshing with Skyrim’s established mechanics, Kallax Storageborn isn’t trying too hard to pretend that its additions are in any way lore-friendly. The first time you’re overencumbered after grabbing the mod, your character is sent a magical talking telegram informing them that a solution to their storage woes can be found in a dungeon called Storereach. Yep, that’s the tone set then.

Storereach starts off as a regular Skyrim cave, but grows into a well-made Dwarven dungeon assembled mostly from recognisable vanilla building blocks. Things really kick into gear when you reach the second level, Storereach Workshop. Here, the standard swells of Skyrim’s orchestral soundtrack morph into the quiet, but unmistakable jingle of distant elevator music as you wander into a Dwarven department store. In case you’re unsure, an apparition materialises to welcome you. If you’re anything like me, you’re completely distracted by the fact that next to him are specially made Dwarven versions of IKEA’s flatbed shopping trollies.

From there, you negotiate a maze of dioramas showing off Dwarven furnishings for different rooms, some of which have buttons you can press to trigger a short demonstration by ghostly salespeople. You learn about Stenrygg seats, Tavan rugs, and Gruskok kitchen sets. The place isn’t just an empty show hall, though: there’s some unique gear and a couple of secrets that are easily missed if you don’t peek around as many corners as you might in a standard dungeon delve. While some of the gags - such as a shield with a deflection enchantment dubbed the ‘Shield of the Returns Policy’ - are rather groan-worthy, a couple properly tickled me. For instance, I stumbled across a skeleton in the loos, bearing a note indicating they’d died after simply getting lost among the labyrinthine halls of the shop. That’s the sort of joke people make about going to IKEA, rather than one the retailers themselves would necessarily make, since it suggests their signage is a bit crap. It’s the sort of touch that stops the creation feeling too reverent or robotic in its efforts to convince you to buy a flat-pack bookcase called Billy, even when it’s giving you a spell that fires the retailer’s famous Swedish meatballs.

The mod’s main draw and namesake awaits in a chamber behind the store. Armed with a tome perfectly mimicking an IKEA instruction manual, and a staff shaped like an allen key, you assemble Kallax. Once its shelves have been inserted, this unit springs to life and starts speaking in comedian Matt Berry’s dulcet tones. He’s a new follower who’ll scrape along the ground behind you as you adventure and carry all of your burdens, much like a certain base game lady whose name rhymes with an STD. Cool. This is about where I expected the adventure to end, once I’d taken one more wander around Storereach to make sure I’d maxed out a loot haul that’s very potent if you rock up at a low level fresh out of Helgen. I can confirm that because I had to start over to try the IKEA mod, as a result of still not having gotten around to making sure my mod load order’s been updated to match last month’s new patch.

Alas, my adventure with Kallax was only beginning. After I’d crafted him his own version of Skyrim’s iconic iron helmet, he had me off to two more dungeons in search first of heirlooms from his missing master, and then in search of an assistant who might be able to shed light on his reason for existence. Along the way, I grew to love not so much Berry’s array of unique lines responding to places I visited and hijinks I got up to, but the more subtly hilarious touch of his footsteps constantly resembling the low rumble of wooden furniture being dragged along stone roads and through grassy undergrowth.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

items.title: “Marvel’s Wolverine” is a Bloody Good Time, Bub
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s
items.text:
Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s long-awaited release of Insomniac’s “Marvel’s Wolverine,” a game with structural echoes of the company’s beloved “Spider-Man” games, with significantly less kid-friendly violence and more linear, intense storytelling. After a prologue/tutorial that feels a bit rocky in storytelling and gameplay, “Wolverine” settles in spectacularly, strapping players into a rollercoaster narrative and telling them not to panic. With remarkably fluid combat, gorgeous graphics, strong voice work, and compelling storytelling, this is one of the best games of 2026, which has already been a remarkably great year for gaming before roughly a dozen more intriguing titles come out before Thanksgiving. The Sony disc drama aside, it’s a good time to be a gamer.

“Marvel’s Wolverine” also owes a wonderful amount to the movies most readers have probably seen about the man with Adamantium bones. At first, it feels like it’s intentionally echoing the excellent “Logan,” the best film about this beloved character, in its sketch of a slightly older Wolverine forced into a protective role for more vulnerable mutants when the evil Bolivar Trask starts kidnapping them. The plan to eradicate mutantkind sends Logan back to his allies at Team X, including founder Nathaniel Essex and familiar faces like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Jean Grey, sketched very differently here than the Sadie Sink version from “BND.” More on that later.

After Team X rescues a group of mutants from Trask’s captivity, including Callisto, “Marvel’s Wolverine” pivots again to incorporate other comic book and film source material. It’s the kind of story that never directly mimics something you’ve seen before, but one can definitely feel the influence of Bryan Singer’s films on Logan’s search for identity and even Jean Grey’s ultimate arc (don’t worry, comic fans—I didn’t just spoil that it goes full Dark Phoenix à la the horrendous “The Last Stand”). As the story moves to Japan, it also brings in some of that country’s influence on this character, as seen cinematically in James Mangold’s underrated “The Wolverine.” You’ll even get to slice and dice your way through hundreds of members of The Hand, also seen in the best action sequence in “Brand New Day.”

And I do mean slice and dice. Parents should be warned that this game is far more violent than they may expect from the developers of “Miles Morales.” The developers don’t dull Logan’s blades in the slightest, allowing you to use them to stab, mutilate, and decapitate on a regular basis. The combat gameplay is familiar in its mix of strike, parry, dodge, and special powers, but it’s as fluid as any game like this that’s ever been released. As techniques, unlike new skills that recharge over time and one improves at the base mechanics, Wolverine becomes almost a Tasmanian Devil of a killing machine, taking enemies out at a rate befitting one of comicdom’s most beloved heroes. It gets to the point where one sees a dozen enemies and doesn’t question how to get through them but wonders why there aren’t more. By the time I got into my New Game Plus playthrough, I had fully mastered the combat of “Wolverine” as much as any game in years, and the adrenaline rush of a perfectly executed move simply never abates. I’ll honestly miss it.

Of course, a game can’t just be about decapitating fools who underestimated a man with claws. As for the rest of the experience, the set pieces are so spectacular that you can forgive the lackluster exploration. As for the latter, Logan often has to find something in a room to push the story forward, which basically just amounts to looking for the white dot that cues you to hit triangle. It’s not exactly thrilling. On the other hand, there are a couple of motorcycle set pieces that are so spectacular that you’ll wish there were more of them, and the big action sequences are as impressive as any MCU movie. The truth is that “Marvel’s Wolverine” gets the big and basic things right; so the minor connective tissue like running around the Team X facility to find the triangle that will push the story forward isn’t really a drag as much as a little break from the intensity before it becomes numbing.

Something else that elevates “Marvel’s Wolverine” over many games of this generation is its attention to environment. As you can imagine, when Logan turns into a blade whirlwind, nothing is safe, and the designers brilliantly allow you to leave a mark, whether it’s just a blade scratch on metal or something more intense. For example, you get into a fight in an arcade in Japan, and no claw machine is safe. Most combat sequences end in the kind of environmental destruction rarely seen in games where you can still take cover behind a wooden box, and it’s the kind of detail that really elevates the overall experience. It should also be noted that this game makes use of the PS5 controller in expansive ways, whether it’s a radio signal or just the hum and buzz of action. And the load times are insanely fast. You can go from startup to combat in actual seconds.

Finally, while “Marvel’s Wolverine” is incredibly fun, it’s also narratively richer than many superhero games. Without spoiling, Logan and Jean Grey become allies not just in stopping the big bad of this game but in figuring out the details of Logan’s lost past. Like in the Singer movies and some of the comic arcs, Logan is a killing machine who doesn’t really know how he got that way, and the script here lands in a place that’s both satisfying and poignant. It’s as rich as the great Uncanny X-Men arcs that this comic book fan grew up loving, and a reminder of how both superhero fiction and gaming can be so much more satisfying when it’s developed with true love, care, and mutilations.

Sony provided a review copy of this game. It is available on September 15, exclusively on PlayStation.

items.title: Bargain with demons and boat with the dead in joyful RPG heist quest anthology Thousand Hells
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the
items.text:
You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the designers of King of Dragon Pass is an absolute tonic. It's a witty procession of Orphic descents, in which you assemble a crew of four garrulous weirdos and pitch them against quest scenarios that might involve talking trees, holy riddlers, and conduits of boiling blood.

There's an infectious, venturesome lightness to the game, which somehow persists alongside dire blunders and supernatural calamities that may see members of your party being cursed, punctured or unhinged. I've only completed a couple of the 10 heists across two hours of play, which makes me reluctant to call this an official review, but it's got my provisional recommendation. Come, reader - get thee to Pandemonium apace.

Watch on YouTube

Thousand Hells doesn't harbour a thousand distinct hells; its variety comes, instead, from choice of party members and the canny reshuffling of story beats, which play out against handsome paintings of monoliths, bazaars, shorelines and catacombs. Each run starts with your character accepting One Last Job from some dubious power-broker in the "Byzantine-flavored" Eternal City. Perhaps you'll be looking into the untimely deaths of some princelings, or maybe you'll be escorting a murderer: either way, you'll need to trek down to an underworld that borrows ideas from Ancient Greece and Mesopotamia.

The opening interview also defines your character, as you pick from backgrounds, strengths and faults. Ho thar! I am Caroline, seasoned sailor and scout, with the bestest biceps this side of the Hungry Sea. My major shortcoming: I like to make jokes about gods.

Having created yourself, you then recruit a crew of similarly imperfect adventurers, spending Question points to decide how much you know about them to begin with. A big hand for Sethre: diplomat, pickpocket and shaman, dream-dogged and impulsive. A round of applause for Hemze: catfooted spymaster, who looks like a bull's derriere. The characters you choose will form loose relationships, reacting to each other's traits as the yarn wears on. These relationships are strongly shaped by the task at hand, which might see you keeping secrets from your colleagues, or deciding in advance that somebody ain't coming back from the Great Below.

The heist itself consists of a series of round-based encounters drawn from a pack of over 280, each with a mix of solutions depending on your party's skillset. In a pleasing tactile device that makes me think yet again of Ursula K Le Guin, encounters are resolved using bags of tokens. Each round, you pull up to four tokens from three bags. You get one bag for the character you've selected to take charge of the encounter (which means you'll be able to play more of their tokens), and one for the rest of the group. A third bag houses tide-turning boons and knowledge you may have acquired by, say, befriending a sorrowful spirit, or jailbreaking a god.

The tokens mostly reflect each character's traits, both helpful and hindersome – "Nerinai is knowledgeable", "Chisu is greedy", "Sethre has a troubled past", "Esanth knows lockpicking". You apply these tokens to one of three actions, corresponding to the scenario. You're navigating the rapids of Styx: do you focus on the rocks, or on the unruly dead crowding the stern? You're helping the Fates weave your very own destiny: do you throw the shuttle, or offer to cut the warp threads?

Other, more generic tokens might grant you resources and buffs, or rid you of debuffs. Show Some Swagger will improve a character's morale, if played successfully, while Get The Measure earns you Insight points, which let you visualise the odds of each token being successful. Any tokens and actions not used up in a round carry over to the next, so you might want to reserve any tokens that could fit several possible actions. Conversely, you'll need to figure out when to dispose of tokens that seem bound to fail. "Hemze is ugly" probably does have a use at some stage – I dunno, maybe Narcissus is working a guard post somewhere, and you can invite him to give Hemze a makeover? - but I'm not sure it's going to help me rescue some drowning merchants.

You need to win a certain number of rounds, and avoid a certain number of losses, but fumbling the encounter doesn't end the game: you might incur an injury or receive a mood penalty, perhaps even lose a character, but you'll often achieve the story objective (like crossing a river) regardless. I've rarely felt the urge to reload a save, which isn't possible anyway.

While never a taut exercise in resource juggling, the encounter design does oblige a bit of strategy, thanks to some underlying combos and questions of timing. Some actions are best performed early, boosting your chances of doing something else – disarming traps before lunging for a treasure, for instance. Some are easier to do when you're ahead or behind on victory points. A few need to be reserved for the encounter's finale.

Sometimes you get a bunch of tokens that don't entirely fit any action, and must guess how the writers will play out the implications. So far, I've found those stabs in the dark more entertaining than jarring, but there have been a couple of moments when the storycraft felt somewhat meaningless, next to the invisible tallying of points. Over the course of the heist, you also need to think about gathering items that serve as quickfix solutions, sometimes allowing you to avoid an encounter.

As you'd expect from the whole "repeatedly going to hell" premise, the encounters can be pretty macabre. During my first run, I had to deal with some hags who can shave away character traits with a nasty look. During my second, I tackled a scenario for which a positive outcome would see a character being hung from a meathook.

There are plague crows, blade tsunamis, and mesmerising demons. Worst of all, there's a poetry contest. (I won the poetry contest, mostly by alternating between mockery of my opponent and flattery of the audience.) As grim as things may get, however, the writing remains brisk and buoyant, with characters squabbling a bit and maybe revealing something about themselves when they strike out, keeping up the momentum of the tale. I've come to love these little setbacks. It's like Scheherazade turning every tumble into a cliffhanger, with her head on the line. It's the kind of game in which a clean sweep feels like a loss, because you've bleached away the reversals and pratfalls that any thrilling adventure should involve.

Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists is out now on Steam. I reckon you should give 'er a go, especially if you enjoyed the art and writing of King of Dragon Pass and its spiritual successor, Six Ages, but found the village management element tedious. I should mention that the game's writers include Holly Nielsen, who has done stuff for RPS in the past.

items.title: TIFF 2026: River, Stuffed, The Housewife
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: Sometimes themes emerge at festivals. Sometimes dispatches like this are merely about what played on the same day, location, or, in this case, both. While
items.text:
Sometimes themes emerge at festivals. Sometimes dispatches like this are merely about what played on the same day, location, or, in this case, both. While Sian Heder’s “Being Heumann” took the coveted spot of Opening Night at the Princess of Wales Theatre, three remarkably different films unfolded across the evening, just down the street at the Royal Alexandra. A horror film, morbid musical, and period drama filled the theatre for three movies in a row, and yours truly was there to report back. Sadly, only one truly made the impact it intended.

What if Leatherface could swim? This was the thought that possibly inspired Joshua Giuliano’s grisly debut, “River,” an IFC effort that should find a blood-loving audience outside of the fest circuit. Two modern-day scream queens in Jane Levy (“Evil Dead”) and Jessica Rothe (“Happy Death Day”) give their fearless, physical all, but the real star here is the sound design and remarkable POV choices that announce newcomer Giuliano as a major genre talent to watch. A lot of the buzz on the ground at TIFF this year has been the question of what could be this fest’s “Obsession”—the Curry Barker film premiered here almost exactly a year ago. “River” is too brutal to make that kinda bank, but it’s the kind of movie that horror fans will truly jump for, something they’ll tell their friends they need to see to believe.

“River” opens with one of its most remarkable scenes. As the camera slowly pans over an empty car with an open trunk, we hear the action that took place before the images on the screen. A couple talks, flirts, listens to music, and then notices someone watching them from the woods. Giuliano and his excellent cinematographer pan across the car from different angles as the sounds of violence fill the soundtrack, sometimes ending on something disturbing like a bloody dent in the car or a human leg. It’s a neat trick, but it’s also an overture to a film that will play with sound and POV in ways that horror often never considers.

The real action of “River” starts with the introduction of tough Lucy (Levy), gentle brother Drew (Max Mattern), and their virtually estranged sister Carla (Rothe). She’s come home after the death of their father, but don’t worry, this isn’t overtly “grief horror,” even if the different relationships these three had with dad feel like they influence their choices as they try to survive the worst night of their lives.

The trio heads out early with dad’s ashes to spread them on his favorite spot on the local river, just past a rickety bridge. After the ceremony, they discover their gas line has ruptured and they’re stuck. Carla swims to shore, but they spot a bloody, shirtless, masked figure before she gets there. From that point on, “River” is relentless, a slasher movie that somehow turns the open space of a river into someplace claustrophobic. You have no gas in your boat, and the shore contains its version of Michael Myers. What the F do you do? It’s the starting point for an insanely brutal journey, one that puts Levy through the wringer nearly as much as “Evil Dead,” and reminds viewers how remarkably physical she can be as a performer.

Levy and Rothe are fantastic, but it’s Giuliano’s use of space and sound that truly elevate “River” above your standard slasher flick. One game he loves to rewardingly play is to have his characters see something before we do—we watch their terrified expression, taking a beat in our own minds to imagine what they could possibly be seeing, before the camera reveals it. It’s remarkably effective, and it’s joined by some of the best genre sound design in years. This movie crunches and breaks in a manner that’s reminiscent of the IFC hit “In a Violent Nature.” With only a few tweaks it could actually have been a sequel to that movie in how it also presents an unkillable force of unimaginable violence through sound design and brutality.

“River” won’t be for everyone—it’s insanely violent—but those who like a slasher pic that isn’t afraid to slash will find so much to admire in a film that doesn’t just play like homage to the ‘70s and ‘80s era when slashers ruled but updates the aesthetics and structure of those films for a new era. The synopsis at TIFF references John Carpenter, which often feels like the kind of standard that does a midnight movie no favors because so few can live up to it. The best compliment I can pay this one is that I think John will dig it.

Theo Rhys’ “Stuffed” should be like shooting roadkill in a barrel for this fan of not just musical theater but morbid humor. Clearly inspired by dark musicals like Sweeney Todd and even Little Shop of Horrors, “Stuffed” is a unique love story with a slowing pulse, a movie about how we all long to be remembered, to do something extraordinary with our ordinary lives. Sadly, despite its captivating concept and influences, along with two committed leads, it’s a misfire, a movie that feels incredibly long at nearly two hours, and one that wastes its performances on characters on a story that never gets under your skin.

Harry Melling continues to impress as Bernie, an ordinary guy who works at the local sandwich factory and cares for a dementia-addled mother. He has absolutely nothing going for him, and he’ll have even less when mom dies. The aesthetic of Bernie’s life reminded me of several Tim Burton characters: oddballs who do their little best to rebel against a world of conformity. What can Bernie possibly do to find his purpose?

When he answers an ad in the paper via a website, he crosses paths with Araminta (Jodie Comer), an equally quirky soul with a morbid hobby. Araminta is a taxidermist, someone who brings home roadkill, skins it, and adds it to her house of silent, unmoving animal friends. She’s waiting on the ultimate prize: A human being. She convinces Bernie that the most extraordinary thing he could do is to live forever in her stuffed menagerie. As they both plan his death, doing things like fake his suicide, they get closer, leading to the question of if, through planning the goodbye for something with nothing, they’ve given him something to live for: Love.

All of this is set to original songs, most of them of the Les Mis sung-dialogue type. Rhys stays close on his talented performers, which allows them to emote through song, but leads to a shockingly flat film visually. There are two numbers with significant choreography—one in the factory with Bernie and another alongside his burning car—and they are easily the standout sequences in the film. I kept wanting the camera to pull back on these performers, to give them a chance to act with their bodies as much as their faces and voices. It leads to a movie that’s remarkably repetitive visually, while also spinning its wheels narratively for way too long. “Stuffed” needed another twist, character, or arc to justify its length. As is, it just feels too hollow.

Finally, there’s the disappointing “The Housewife,” a film that sadly fails a test of a fictional take on a true story in that a documentary about this subject would almost certainly be significantly more interesting. The biggest problem is that director Ben Shirinian never finds a visual language for this period drama, shooting it like a TV movie instead of a theatrical feature. Naomi Watts does her absolute best, but she gets lost in a character that screenwriter Alyssa Hill never quite figured out. On the one hand, Hermine Braunsteiner would be difficult for anyone to unpack, but Shirinian is too content to keep her as a mystery for the first half of the film and an unspeakable villain for the second. The result is a movie that has no real identity, not in character, visual, or theme.

Watts plays Hermine Ryan, a New York woman in Queens in the ‘60s. She’s the pillar of her community, admired by her neighbors and loved by her husband Russell (Luke Evans). When the New York Times gets a tip from Elie Wiesenthal that the Ryan house is hiding a Nazi right in a New York City borough, writer Joseph Lelyveld (Tye Sheridan) goes to the house to talk to Russell, falling for Hermine’s warmth and excellent oatmeal raisin cookies. Of course, it’s barely a spoiler to reveal that it’s not Russell that the Times, and eventually the U.S. Government (personified here by an immigration officer played by Michael Imperioli), should worry about: It’s “The Mare,” a female guard at Majdanek given that name because of how much she liked to kick prisoners. She was the first Nazi extradited from the United States, accused of collaborating in the murders of over 1,000 people.

Watts is most interesting in scenes in which she allows The Mare to sneak through the façade that she has created as a perfect immigrant wife. At first, she totally denies the charges, but Watts allows us to peek at the evil barely concealed underneath. Despite how the screenplay forces her to play aspects of Hermine that feel tailored to the movie more than real, Watts makes choices that shine through.

There’s not much to praise about the rest. It’s one of those historical dramas that means well, one that thinks the power of the true story will do the heavy lifting, but questions like what this narrative means in 2026 or how to make it visually engaging were never asked. The idea that a child-murdering Nazi could become a beloved Queens housewife is a fascinating one. But a movie needs to be more than just an idea.

When the New York Times gets a tip from Elie Wiesenthal that the Ryan house is hiding a Nazi right in a New York City borough, writer Joseph Lelyveld (Tye Sheridan) goes to the house to talk to Russell, falling for Hermine’s warmth and excellent oatmeal raisin cookies. Of course, it’s barely a spoiler to reveal that it’s not Russell that the Times, and eventually the U.S. Government (personified here by an immigration officer played by Michael Imperioli), should worry about: It’s “The Mare,” a female guard at Majdanek given that name because of how much she liked to kick prisoners. She was the first Nazi extradited from the United States, accused of collaborating in the murders of over 1,000 people.

Watts is most interesting in scenes in which she allows The Mare to sneak through the façade that she has created as a perfect immigrant wife. At first, she totally denies the charges, but Watts allows us to peek at the evil barely concealed underneath. Despite how the screenplay forces her to play aspects of Hermine that feel tailored to the movie more than real, Watts makes choices that shine through.

There’s not much to praise about the rest. It’s one of those historical dramas that means well, one that thinks the power of the true story will do the heavy lifting, but questions like what this narrative means in 2026 or how to make it visually engaging were never asked. The idea that a child-murdering Nazi could become a beloved Queens housewife is a fascinating one. But a movie needs to be more than just an idea.

items.title: "We track every server you enter": the Wardogs devs are "coming down hard" on XP farms and cash exploits, even as they encourage people to grind
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game
items.text:
The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game currency and XP, or who spend “more than a few minutes” in servers created for this purpose.

Given that Wardogs advertises itself as a shooter about getting rich – a game in which "cash is king", with individualised payouts for a bunch of different in-game actions - I do feel like Bulkhead are sending mixed messages, even by the standards of incoherent wargames. Trying to define 'fairly earned' in a game that encourages you to be a frenzied, gun-toting plutomaniac is surely plunging headfirst into farce. Mind you, I respect the desire to Maintain The Fun for players who aren't quite as dollar-driven, and avoid having a community browser slammed with servers called "[EU/DOGF$RM]" or similar.

Wardogs launched in early access last week, reaching an audience of over 400,000 simultaneous Steam players by Sunday. James spent some time in it last week, and returned with many thrilling gigwork anecdotes. The devs have now rolled out a patch aimed at improving the game's server browser, with a new dedicated feed for community servers.

"Community Servers are the lifeblood of FPS games like ours," they write on Steam. "We want to make sure we actively create technology in and out of the game that supports the growth and fostering of communities. We have failed to do that by rushing our Community Server strategy. As we've always said, when we're wrong, we'll hold our hands up. We got this bit wrong." In addition to the update, the devs are giving players in community servers an additional 5% End of Match cash bonus by way of apology. "So if you're looking to grind, we suggest jumping in a community server."

These heartwarming sentiments about server grinding go hand in hand with a blood-chilling threat against those who create or join servers purely in order to crank out XP by mindlessly repeating actions. "The economy of WARDOGS interlinks all players together into one shared universe and experience, even more so when we bring the meta into the game," the devs write. "As an early access game, we're not perfect, and we never will be. But if you do find something and take advantage of it, we have decided to come down hard."

Players who "abuse cash exploits and bugs" will have their cash and XP reset to zero. You'll also get a timed ban, depending on previous infractions. People who make "content that tutorialises how to abuse systems, with no regard for reporting the issue" will be treated "as advertising cheats", and will receive a permanent ban. The wording here is a bit muddy, but it sounds like they're telling us not to share details about cash/XP exploits, unless we're genuinely trying to report an issue to the devs. "We are not saying do not post on social media or Discord," the devs write. "We are saying there is a difference between promoting and alerting."

And people who launch or make use of XP server farms? For you Bulkhead have unlocked the very lowest echelons of Banhammer Hell. "We track every server you enter, and we are also very aware of which servers are XP farming servers," they write. "If your account is tracked as joining one of these servers for more than a few minutes, we will ban your account permanently."

Bulkhead promise that even if you're currently getting away with abusing a system, they'll catch up to you eventually. "Effectively, if you find something and you then keep doing it, over and over again, that is abuse of an exploit," they conclude. "If you figure something out and test it once or twice, no biggy, thanks for helping us QA."

Bulkhead are hardly unique in wanting people to obsess over an in-game earning loop, but not to the extent that they take the logical next step, game the system, and mess up the experience for other players. The creators of Destiny have had this discussion a billion times over. It just amuses me a bit more in a game that has all this edgelord materialism up front. It's a dog-eat-dog world out there but stop that! Bad dog! You must play by the agreed rules. Anyway: have you spent any time in Wardogs? I don't know if James plans to keep up his combat taxi-driving career.

items.title: TIFF 2026: Woman Unknown, Lemonade, The Julia Set
items.author: Marya E. Gates
items.summary: This year’s Centerpiece and Special Presentations section of the Toronto International Film Festival featured a striking postwar drama from Danish-Egyptian
items.text:
This year’s Centerpiece and Special Presentations section of the Toronto International Film Festival featured a striking postwar drama from Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy, a tender narrative debut from documentarian Kim Bartley, and the follow-up film from last year’s breakout star Chase Infiniti.

Venice Film Festival Golden Lion winner “Woman Unknown,” the latest from writer-director May el-Touky, immerses you directly in the psyche of a woman doing her best to survive post-WWII Danish society. Before we meet Marie (Mathilde Arcel, who also took home the Volpi Cup at Venice for her shattering performance), we’re introduced to the haunting specter of the woman who came before her. The fabric of a silk wedding dress cascades through the darkness, the moon illuminating its pristine, white sheen. Marie awakes before the sun rises, leaving her partner to his slumber. We soon learn she is a maid and nanny in this well-to-do household. She’s also on the cusp of marrying her boss, rising above her station to become the new lady of the house.

Anyone in this position would already be walking on eggshells, but in Marie’s case she’s also harboring a dark secret from her past during the German occupation of Denmark. Like many women, she did what she had to do to survive. As the film progresses, we learn she’s haunted not just by the fear that her past will be exposed and, like other women branded collaborators, she’ll be violently stripped in the street, her hair shorn like a sheep, and her body painted with a red swastika, but also with physical pain and a personal anguish that will never leave her. The film is punctuated by several sequences of these women being violently humiliated in the streets, with el-Touky holding her camera on their faces as they are dehumanized. In one such interlude, the actress at the center evokes the great Falconetti in Dreyer’s “The Passion of Joan of Arc.”

El-Touky’s deft script not only exposes the hypocrisy of a society that is so quick to punish these women but turns a blind eye on the businessmen like her fiancé who continued operating—and selling to Germans—during the occupation. It also explores the way in which for many women, occupation or no, their bodies do not belong to them. Staying uncomfortably close to Marie’s battered psyche, this is a brutal film about the insidious violence of occupation, the many ways we can lose our humanity, and a sharp rumination on whether or not resilience is always admirable.

With her first narrative feature film, documentarian Kim Bartley’s “Lemonade” is a tender, if somewhat cliched, look at perseverance in the face of a hard childhood. Lewis Brophy stars as Danny, a young man who’s been in the social services system most of his childhood. Separated from his brother for years and just shy of his 18th birthday, Danny makes a bad choice that lands him in jail. After turning eighteen, not only does he have to leave the youth home where he’s been living for the past few years, he also faces his court date as an adult.

Just as Danny must face the world on his own for the first time, Josh (Barry Keoghan, soulful as always), the caseworker who he thinks is responsible for his separation from his brother, re-enters his life. The two have much in common; Josh and his older brother also went through the system as kids. Like Danny’s mother, Josh’s older brother Gav (Graham Earley) is an addict. The film is at its strongest when it explores the similarities–and pointed differences–between these two sets of brothers. Unfortunately, the script teeters between exposition heavy dialogue and cliched plot points that pull down its otherwise clear-eyed vision of Danny’s world.

A side plot involving a girl named Mila (Carla Tous), who is unfortunately little more than a Gen Z twist on the manic pixie dream girl trope. She’s got a magic bag that seems to have everything you might need at any given moment (including batteries??) and even has a tattoo on her arm that reads: When life gives you lemons; make lemonade. Brophy and Tous have very little chemistry, and their scenes together fit incongruously with the emotional journey Danny is on with Josh, with his estranged mother, and most importantly with the little brother he so desperately wants to reconnect with. That said, the final reunion between the brothers is staged so beautifully, it could make a stone cry.

Following up her breakout turn in Paul Thomas Anderson’s Oscar-winning “One Battle After Another,” Chicago’s own Chase Infiniti stars as a young math whiz who finds herself in a bad romance during her freshman year of college in Nicki Byrne’s “The Julia Set”. Set at a fictional called GBU, Infiniti is the titular Julia, a promising young mathematician who chose a school near home instead of the many spots she’d earned at Ivy League schools in order to be near her family and her older brother, who has Down Syndrome.

She soon stands out among her peers and is tapped by her TA Pascal (Christopher Birney) to join an elite study group led by a brilliant, award-winning professor (Nina Hoss) as they prepare to take the Putnam Exam, which could help define all of their futures. For Julia, this could mean a full ride to one of her dream schools. For Pascal, it’s his chance to prove the apple didn’t fall that far from the tree; his father (Jason Isaacs), we soon learn, is an overbearing Fields Medal winner who has a building named after him on campus, and has also done on a number on Pascal’s self-worth.

Julia is clearly much more naturally gifted than Pascal, and I winced the first time she made herself smaller so he could get the spotlight. As their relationship gets more intense, his jealousy of her talent manifests in more and more violent and manipulative ways. While their story arc borders on cliche, Byrne finds a refreshing way for Julia to come into her own.

Birney is an interesting young actor, who brought a lot of depth and sensitivity to his breakout role as Conrad in the streaming hit “The Summer I Turned Pretty,” and brings a similar complexity to a role that could have just been a stereotype. Infiniti imbues Julia with a rich interiority largely through her sharp eyes and body language. Gillian Anderson is perhaps a little under-used as Pascal’s mother, who let her own light dampen so her husband’s alleged genius could shine, but she gives one hell of speech to knock some sense into Julia that, while didactic, is something a lot of young women need to hear: Live your life for yourself while you’re young. There will be plenty of time to make compromises later on.

items.text:
The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for realising that after playing The Blood of Dawnwalker, you've developed a craving for blackcurrant juice. There's none in the cupboard, so you venture out to get some, floating across the rooftops as a trail of mist as you go. You arrive at the supermarket, fangs bared and claws out. You parry and dodge attackers armed with trollies as you fight your way up the aisles. There it is. The sweet crimson nectar. You reach out to grab a bottle. A hand reaches out through the display and grips your wrist.

"Brencis?" you cry out. There's no answer. Instead, the strange appendage begins to drag you along the aisle at warp speed, knocking off bottles which thunk and bump against your face as they fall. "Stoooooooooooppppppppppp," you cry as the a black eye begins to form where a cola bottle got you good. Surprisingly, the rogue arm obeys. However, it doesn't loosen its grip. Blinking away spilled beverages, you find yourself face-to-face with a label. Steve Ballmer Betrayed His Fellow Billionaires, And They Are Not Pleased, it reads. It's made by a company called Defector and seems to contain commentary on the Los Angeles Clippers being slapped for violating the NBA's rules on paying basketball players.

The sleazy-funny particulars aside, this story and the extraordinary penalty the Clippers and Ballmer received are ultimately about a group of the other 29 franchise operators, maybe even all of them, policing their cohort's conduct. Some of those owners helped midwife Ballmer into the group 12 years ago when Donald Sterling finally disgraced his way out of ownership. They are getting theirs back, not because they all wanted Leonard to play on their team—that would mean competing for a prize, which few of them prioritize above collecting their revenues—but because Ballmer unclogged his nostrils on the salary cap, which is both practically and conceptually the grand underpinning of their profitability.

As soon as you're done reading, the arm takes off once more. You're dragged down the soup aisle, tins ricocheting to and fro. Before you know it, your face is covered in a thick mask of baked beans. "No, helpppp, stopppppppp," you yell through the orange haze. The appendage complies again. A packet stands before you. The Blood of Dawnwalker's lack of stealth makes this Witcher 3-like feel incomplete, its label reads. Ooh, a take from GamesRadar foodmaker Fran Ruiz that you're not sure you agree with, but know others who certainly might.

As we've seen in other open-world games with infamy systems, there's no easy answer to the dilemma of properly reacting to players' chaotic actions in ways that both preserves the credibility of the established narrative and dynamically raises the challenge. Coen is a unique kind of menace, though. Whether day or at night, he's charging into conflict, sword out, ready for a proper melee. Even when he's walking around the city of Svartrau, he doesn't seem to mind being recognized until it's too late. I know he's no Agent 47 or Ezio Auditore, but this disconnect makes me wish The Blood of Dawnwalker had even more friction baked in.

Woosh. You're yanked off again (not like that). Things start to smell a bit more earthy. Oh bugger, the fruit and veg section! Soon, you're being slapped with apples and creamed by bananas. "Pleeeesseee, scccchhhhhtttoopppp", you mumble through a mouth nearly plugged up by a loose turnip. All is still. Before you sits a marrow. On its label are the words 'Petit Planet's latest build brings Pokopia-inspired elements to Animal Crossing in space'. You notice that this particular bit of veg has seemingly been reserved for a Rebecca Jones of Respec, which you assume to be nearby town.

Turns out things aren't all smooth sailing for this jellyfish girl who has decided to go and live on land, and the quest was a surprisingly heartfelt examination of both emotional and physical homesickness, tasking the protagonist with learning to cook some of Nerina's favourite seafoods and – at one point – literally fish her out of the museum's ocean exhibit after she hurls herself in during a fit of delirium, which honestly got a bit darker than I'd been expecting.

The world becomes a blur once more. Things start to get cold. The frozen section beckons. You make peace with the fact you might be about to die of hypothermia amid a sea of 3 for 2 signs. Shards of ice skitter aside as your skin begins to numb. You have just enough energy to beg in whispers for the arm to stop once and for all. It does. A box offers you instructions as to How to throw a LAN party in 2026. Why's this in the frozen section? Ah, it's made by Morgan Park of Perfectly Cold Gamer.

It was comfortably the best birthday party I've had as an adult. I was worried at first that going to all this trouble to play stuff that we could more easily set up over Discord would end up feeling pointless, but that was quickly disproven: Everything about playing shooters with your buds is more fun when they're actually in the room emoting, reacting, and trash-talking to your face. I want to make this a more regular thing, but honestly, it wasn't a smooth ride. We had issues both technical and logistical—some self-inflicted, some harder to predict. We really could've used a LAN veteran on the scene.

Suddenly the arm pulls you head-first into the depths of a freezer. The cold is everywhere and it's overwhelming. You realise that the arm belongs to a bald man who's curled up next you. "Brencis?" you ask again.

"Yes," the vampire baddie from The Blood of Dawnwalker says.

"What are you doing here?"

"It's a long stor-"

Before he can finish, the freezer opens and you're both yanked out. The pair of you end up laid out on a trolley atop a mound of frozen peas. Gazing down at you is the face of Adrian Edmondson. He takes off pushing at warp speed, laughing maniacally while the pair of you hold on for dear life and some Witchery tunes play over the tannoy.

"Pleeeesseee, scccchhhhhtttoopppp", you mumble through a mouth nearly plugged up by a loose turnip. All is still. Before you sits a marrow. On its label are the words 'Petit Planet's latest build brings Pokopia-inspired elements to Animal Crossing in space'. You notice that this particular bit of veg has seemingly been reserved for a Rebecca Jones of Respec, which you assume to be nearby town.

Turns out things aren't all smooth sailing for this jellyfish girl who has decided to go and live on land, and the quest was a surprisingly heartfelt examination of both emotional and physical homesickness, tasking the protagonist with learning to cook some of Nerina's favourite seafoods and – at one point – literally fish her out of the museum's ocean exhibit after she hurls herself in during a fit of delirium, which honestly got a bit darker than I'd been expecting.

The world becomes a blur once more. Things start to get cold. The frozen section beckons. You make peace with the fact you might be about to die of hypothermia amid a sea of 3 for 2 signs. Shards of ice skitter aside as your skin begins to numb. You have just enough energy to beg in whispers for the arm to stop once and for all. It does. It was comfortably the best birthday party I've had as an adult. I was worried at first that going to all this trouble to play stuff that we could more easily set up over Discord would end up feeling pointless, but that was quickly disproven: Everything about playing shooters with your buds is more fun when they're actually in the room emoting, reacting, and trash-talking to your face. I want to make this a more regular thing, but honestly, it wasn't a smooth ride. We had issues both technical and logistical—some self-inflicted, some harder to predict. We really could've used a LAN veteran on the scene.

Suddenly the arm pulls you head-first into the depths of a freezer. The cold is everywhere and it's overwhelming. You realise that the arm belongs to a bald man who's curled up next you. "Brencis?" you ask again.
"Yes," the vampire baddie from The Blood of Dawnwalker says.
"What are you doing here?"
"It's a long stor-"

Before he can finish, the freezer opens and you're both yanked out. The pair of you end up laid out on a trolley atop a mound of frozen peas. Gazing down at you is the face of Adrian Edmondson. He takes off pushing at warp speed, laughing maniacally while the pair of you hold on for dear life and some Witchery tunes play over the tannoy.

items.text:
In this year’s Discovery and Platform sections at the Toronto International Film Festival, I saw three films about women navigating their twenties, their artistic ambitious, and their interpersonal relationships with their closest friends: Alexandra Pechman’s “Magazine,” Nyla Innuksuk’s “In The Heart of the South,” and Irene Dionisio’s “Idda.” Two of these films are far more successful at processing the growing pains of your twenties through the lens of cinema than the third.

Following up her debut 2022 alien invasion debut “Slash/Back,” writer-director Nyla Innuksuk’s doesn’t totally pivot away from genre filmmaking, although she does have plenty to say about why certain stories are only allowed to be told through the lens of genre. “In The Heart of The South,” a title that is in reference to Toronto being south of the arctic from which its main Inuk protagonist Yura Ivalu (Anna Lambe) hails. Yura is the current it girl of the Toronto art world after her immersive virtual reality piece about residential schools shoots her to stardom.

A few film offers follow. In one meeting Yura has the opportunity to adapt an Inuit novel that will help teach white audiences; the other company is less up front with their well-meaning racism, claiming they want to platform Yura’s personal story — just it has to have genre hook. But really, it’s her story they assure her. As she frantically attempts to write an outline based on a traumatic story from her childhood, her estranged friend Sesi (Zorga Qaunaq) re-enters her life, and soon the truth about their shared past comes back to haunt her.

Yura has no qualms about commodifying her culture for the great good, when she’s the only Native artist in the room. However, as soon as Sesi enters the picture, not only does Yura begin to question her own “Inuit-ness,” she begins to spiral about her talent as an artist as well. Like Yura’s VR piece, Innuksuk uses immersive sound design to bring the audience into her psychosis. As Yura’s self-doubt grows, it also manifests as rashes on her skin, showing for the whole world her insecurities.

Qaunaq is deeply ominous as Sesi, while also being wonderfully mordant. As the tides turn on Yura and Sesi’s strange behavior begins to make more sense, both actresses manage to ground the more melodramatic elements of the plot in sincere emotionality. Innuksuk’s razor sharp satire bites not only into the white guilt ridden art and film world that’s more than ready to exploit Indigenous pain for profit, but also those Indigenous artists who are willing to sell their pain – and the pain of their communities – to the highest bidder in the name of speaking “the truth.”

In Irene Dionisio’s dizzying drama “Idda,” two women reconnect in their hometown of Catania in Sicily during the festival of Festival of Saint Agatha with plans to climb to the top of Mount Etna. Idda, we learn, is the feminine name given by the locals to the active volcano. Adele (Tecla Insolia) is a photographer, whose mother passed away a few years ago. Sofia (Romana Maggiora Vergano) is a dance teacher and free spirit. As these two women crash back into each other’s lives, Dionisio continually flashes to the volcano, its grey ash and red molten lava, destroying in its beautiful path. Cinematographer Gergely Pohárnok brings a rich and tactile texture to this world, while the film’s sound design wholly transports the viewer into the realm of the mountain.

As the women make their way up the mountain, a strange resentment bubbles between them. Dionisio allows this fissure to rumble without quite exploding for most of the film, much like the mountain itself. It’s alive, but under the surface. And while the final reveal at the end of the film doesn’t quite work, the film’s immersive world almost makes up for the distance we’re kept from these characters. Dionisio also does a wonderful job of bringing the local festival back to its pagan roots, contrasting the procession of the candalora of Saint Agatha to an altar up on the mountain for the nymph Aetna, who is said to have carried her child to term on the volcano’s peak.

Time, like the volcano’s ash, will come for everyone and everything, even if you’re able to capture a moment of it with a photograph. As the film progresses, Adele must learn to live with the ghosts of her past, and feel the warmth of the memories that remain, because even the painful ones remind us of what once was, and what still remains.

Sometimes at a festival like TIFF you discover a bold new voice with a distinct point of view or singular cinematic vision. Other times you watch a first time director and wonder if they’re even a storyteller, let alone a filmmaker. Unfortunately Alexandra Pechman’s debut film “Magazine” falls in the latter category. Set in 2011, the film follows Arizona transplant and wannabe poet Nora (Lily McInerny, whose wide eyes aren’t enough to add texture or internality to the hollowness of her character) during her stint as an unpaid summer intern at Platen, a fictional prestigious quarterly lit journal a la The Paris Review or Granta.

Early on she makes it clear she does not come from money, unlike it’s implied most of the young people who are able to live and work in NYC unpaid are. However, the economic disparity of Nora’s situation with her peers and the way this system weeds out working class youth is not really touched on again beyond a broadly stereotyped “writer actress model” rich girl who can’t utter a word without dropping the name of a famous person. Nora quickly finds herself in a situationship with Thomas (Joshuah Melnick), the associate editor who hired her, the power dynamics of which are only briefly addressed towards the end of the film. Delaney Rowe, who terminally online folks might know from her satirical rom com videos, has a cameo as the managing editor of the mag that proves just because you can make people laugh for 60 seconds online does not mean who can actually act

There are also brief moments within this literary milieu that aim for satire by falling embarrassingly short of the mark. For a character who claims to want to be a writer, we barely get a hint at what Noa has to say or worse why she even wants to be a poet. If the film had even vaguely hinted that it was about how at twenty-two you still need to find your voice, that would have been cliche, but at least it would have been some kind of arc. Instead we get a whole lot of nothing. All the characters are either painted in the broadest strokes, or left completely undeveloped; never once did I care about the emotional stakes of any of these characters.

Along with the poor writing, Pechman’s filmmaking itself leaves much to be desired. The dramatic tension is inert, leaning heavily on montage and soundtrack to move things forward. The sound edits are incompetent, with most songs ending abruptly, without any editorial thrust as to why. Ultimately, it’s a New York movie that makes New York seem incredibly insular and boring. It’s a film that is perhaps so specific it never manages to strike on any universal feeling nor find any kind of wisdom or truth. As for its period setting, if you’re nostalgic for your BlackBerry or Peter Pan collars, maybe that would elicit an emotion beyond boredom. Alas, I mostly just felt relief. . .when the film finally ended.

items.text:
A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten pounds, the artifacts are estimated to be 1,000 years old and constitute Finland’s largest coin hoard of the era

A metal detectorist in southern Finland has unearthed the country’s largest hoard of Late Iron Age silver coins to date. Buried in the 11th century in what’s now the town of Sysmä, the ten-pound collection contains remnants of jewelry and likely thousands of coins.

The detectorist, Kalle Lappinen, was scanning ground in his hometown last week when his metal detector signaled. He began digging, and then his handheld probe “roared,” Lappinen tells the New York Times’ Ephrat Livni.

“With the fury of a monkey, I dug through the soil, bottom moraine and cobblestones,” he recalls. He found “a pile of coins” about 18 inches down and, once he had “recovered from the adrenaline rush,” reported it to authorities. Then, not far away, Lappinen’s metal detector signaled again, prompting him to dig a second hole—and find yet another trove of coins.

Did you know? The Staffordshire Hoard

One of the most famous discoveries by a metal detectorist was made in 2009, when Terry Herbert unearthed an astonishing

cache of some 3,500 pieces of early medieval gold and silver metalwork in Staffordshire, England, that were eventually valued at more than $5 million.

The next day, Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist at the nearby Lahti City Museums, arrived to inspect and excavate the artifacts. According to a statement from the museums, the collection includes a fragment of hacksilver, a silver bracelet, a silver charm, a silver bead and many silver coins—which have not yet been cleaned, separated or counted. The coins alone weigh just under ten pounds; experts say there must be thousands.

“There are quite a lot of coins in this hoard,” and they await detailed analysis, Tikkala tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe. “There will definitely be scientific articles published on the hoard as a whole, as well as more detailed studies of the coins themselves.”

The hoard likely dates to between about 1000 and 1050 C.E., Tikkala says. This half-century corresponds with the tail end of the Viking Age, which historians typically confine to about 793 C.E.—when Vikings raided Lindisfarne in Britain—through 1066, the date of the Norman Conquest. Lahti City Museums have thus classified the hoard as a “Viking Age” find.

“The term ‘Viking Age’ does not imply that there were Vikings in Finland,” Tikkala explains. “We have no sources suggesting that Finland was ‘Viking’ in the same sense as regions of present-day Sweden, Norway and Denmark.”

Though Finland isn’t Scandinavian and wasn’t Viking territory, by the 11th century, some Swedes had settled on its southern coasts. As Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums, tells the Times, “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers—some of whom were indeed Vikings—across the Baltic Sea.”

The silver hoard found by Lappinen was buried in two birch-bark containers, about 40 feet apart, per the statement. Experts don’t know why it was buried, but historians do know that the close of the Viking Age was an unstable period in Finland, as Swedes and Danes raided its regions where Finns, Russians and Germans traded.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” Paukku tells the Times, citing societal unrest due to external threats. “One can only say that whoever they”—the people who hid the silver—“were, they did not come back to collect the treasure. … No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Lappinen’s find marks the latest in a remarkable tally of silver discoveries this year. Just over a week ago, a Dane landscaping in his backyard accidentally unearthed Denmark’s largest hoard of Viking silver, and in April, metal detectorists in Norway found their country’s largest deposit of Viking silver. The Sysmä collection has easily taken the title of Finland’s largest silver coin hoard, which previously belonged to a five-pound stash unearthed near the southern coast in 1895.

The Sysmä discovery is “a case of responsible and responsive detecting, which has produced a promising archaeological discovery,” Eljas Oksanen, an archaeologist at the University of Helsinki, tells the Times. It shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to.”
